source.authors: Ren J, Mo W, Zhang H, He R, Wang X, Jiang T, Liu Y
source.title: The light-independent locomotion response to a static magnetic field in Xenopus tadpoles

value: In bright light the magnet cut swimming distance by 31% and speed by 32%; active swimming duration did not change
method: behavioural: swimming distance, speed and active duration under a static magnet versus sham
conditions: Xenopus tadpoles stage 48 (species named X. laevis in the Introduction; Methods print 'Xenopus tadpoles (stage 48)'); real-time tracking, 5 min dark adaptation then 30 s light pulse to trigger swimming; static magnet (NdFeB stacks wrapped in tin foil) against a sham of tin-foil-wrapped nickel coins; field in blank and sham arenas 0.042 +/- 0.001 and 0.043 +/- 0.005 mT (geomagnetic level 0.04-0.06 mT), magnet arenas a gradient of 0.1-30 mT (arenas 1, 2, 5, 6) and 0.1-80 mT (arenas 3, 4); at least six independent experiments with 12-18 tadpoles each; the response is to a strong static field and its gradient, so it does not show a compass or the receptor; bright-light condition
quote: Under the bright conditions, tadpoles maintained a similar active swimming duration, but swimming intensity, i.e., distance (−31%, p = 0.0025) and swimming speed (−32%, p = 0.0015), was significantly inhibited by the presence of the magnet (Figure 3C).
note: Null result kept in the value: no change in active duration in bright light. The same paper reports a 26% fall in active duration during the dark pulse (separate record).

source.authors: Ren J, Mo W, Zhang H, He R, Wang X, Jiang T, Liu Y
source.title: The light-independent locomotion response to a static magnetic field in Xenopus tadpoles

value: During the 30 s dark pulse the magnet cut swimming distance by 26%, active duration by 26% and speed by 32%
method: behavioural: swimming distance, speed and active duration under a static magnet versus sham, after dark adaptation
conditions: Xenopus tadpoles stage 48 (species named X. laevis in the Introduction; Methods print 'Xenopus tadpoles (stage 48)'); real-time tracking, 5 min dark adaptation then 30 s light pulse to trigger swimming; static magnet (NdFeB stacks wrapped in tin foil) against a sham of tin-foil-wrapped nickel coins; field in blank and sham arenas 0.042 +/- 0.001 and 0.043 +/- 0.005 mT (geomagnetic level 0.04-0.06 mT), magnet arenas a gradient of 0.1-30 mT (arenas 1, 2, 5, 6) and 0.1-80 mT (arenas 3, 4); at least six independent experiments with 12-18 tadpoles each; the response is to a strong static field and its gradient, so it does not show a compass or the receptor; 30 s dark pulse after dark adaptation
quote: All three locomotion parameters showed statistical significance decreased during the 30s dark pulse (distance: − 26%, p = 0.0011; active duration: − 26%, p = 0.0155; speed: − 32%, p = 0.0007) (Figure 3D).
note: The authors read the response in the dark as light-independent (Abstract).

value: Total number of path adjustments fell 34% in bright light and 55% in the dark under the magnet
method: behavioural: counts of path directional adaptations under a static magnet versus sham
conditions: Xenopus tadpoles stage 48 (species named X. laevis in the Introduction; Methods print 'Xenopus tadpoles (stage 48)'); real-time tracking, 5 min dark adaptation then 30 s light pulse to trigger swimming; static magnet (NdFeB stacks wrapped in tin foil) against a sham of tin-foil-wrapped nickel coins; field in blank and sham arenas 0.042 +/- 0.001 and 0.043 +/- 0.005 mT (geomagnetic level 0.04-0.06 mT), magnet arenas a gradient of 0.1-30 mT (arenas 1, 2, 5, 6) and 0.1-80 mT (arenas 3, 4); at least six independent experiments with 12-18 tadpoles each; the response is to a strong static field and its gradient, so it does not show a compass or the receptor; bright and dark conditions
quote: The total number of path directional adaptations were significantly reduced in both the bright (−34%, p = 0.0015) and dark (−55%, p = 0.0001) conditions under the SMF (Figures 4A,B) …
note: Quote cut after the parenthesis; the omitted tail reads 'consistent with our hypothesis above, and the reduction are greater than that of the three locomotion parameters analyzed above.'

value: burrow axes oriented along the North-South axis (second-order mean)
method: field: second-order (species mean) axial direction of long straight tunnel segments; magnetoreception inferred, not tested
conditions: field data: 68 burrow systems charted in earlier studies and provided to the authors (Abstract; Table 1 lists n by species and locality); axial burrow directions measured with a digital compass rose and normalised to magnetic north, tested with Rayleigh tests; observational and correlational, no manipulation of the field, so other directional cues (slope, soil, sun, drainage) are not excluded; the authors write 'We suggest' that the Earth's magnetic field acts as a heading indicator; silvery mole-rat (Table 1 gives 'Silvery mole-rat (Heliophobius argenteocinereus)'), solitary, n = 31 burrow systems (Table 1)

source.authors: Malewski S, Begall S, Schleich CE, Antenucci CD, Burda H
source.title: Do subterranean mammals use the Earth's magnetic field as a heading indicator to dig straight tunnels?

quote: An axial directional preference for the North–South axis was observed for the silvery mole-rat (Fig. 1A), while it was slightly shifted to NNW/SSE in the Talas tuco-tuco (Fig. 1B).
note: The sentence also names the Talas tuco-tuco, logged on its own record. The preceding sentence of the paper says a significant deviation from random orientation was found at second order for the silvery mole-rat, and that at the level of single burrow systems 90% of H. argenteocinereus systems deviated significantly. Contrast in the same paper: Spalax galili burrows showed no prevailing magnetic direction. Grade g because the sense is presumed from burrow direction.

source.authors: Hoover H, Manenti R, Melotto A
source.title: The Role of Experience in the Visual and Non-Visual Prey Recognition of Fire Salamander Populations from Caves and Streams

value: after 55 days of rearing, approach time in tests with a visual stimulus (odourless plastic-string decoy) fell by more than 170 s
method: behavioural: time of approach to a prey stimulus before and after rearing, visual cue versus chemical cue
conditions: larvae (developmental stage 1) from seven caves and six streams in the Italian Prealps of Lombardy, 52 larvae collected (per-population n not given in the Methods); tests in daylight at about 500 lux; visual-only condition used an uncoloured, odourless plastic-string decoy moved with shaking tweezers; larvae were reared individually for 55 days at a mean 18 C under natural photoperiods and fed while exposed to accompanying stimuli, so the post-rearing change reflects experience, not an innate response
quote: After rearing, for the tests including a visual stimulus, there was a reduction in the average approach time by more than 170 s (Figure 3, Table 2).
note: Tests 'including a visual stimulus' as the sentence says; chemical cue (defrosted Chironomus larva) and visual cue were also tested separately and the Abstract states both cues significantly affected approach time. The species is the paper's subject (title; Diversity record), the quoted sentence does not name it.

source.authors: Hoover H, Manenti R, Melotto A
source.title: The Role of Experience in the Visual and Non-Visual Prey Recognition of Fire Salamander Populations from Caves and Streams

value: no difference in approach time between cave and stream larvae
method: behavioural: time of approach to prey stimuli, cave-origin versus stream-origin larvae
conditions: larvae (developmental stage 1) from seven caves and six streams in the Italian Prealps of Lombardy, 52 larvae collected (per-population n not given in the Methods); tests in daylight at about 500 lux; visual-only condition used an uncoloured, odourless plastic-string decoy moved with shaking tweezers; larvae were reared individually for 55 days at a mean 18 C under natural photoperiods and fed while exposed to accompanying stimuli, so the post-rearing change reflects experience, not an innate response
quote: No differences between cave and stream larvae were observed.
note: Null result. The Discussion states that larvae origin had no detectable effect on approach time with the different stimuli (visual and chemical). The quoted sentence does not name the species.
